title: Signing Request (ZIFFER-SPEC-001 §9.1.1, RAD-3 / RAD-4)
description:
What the KMS receives from the Policy Engine. It is the only artifact that crosses leg F3.2 of the leg register (ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 Annex A), and it carries one thing: the canonical bytes the KMS is being asked to sign with the `receipt_signing_key` (§9.1.1 step 6).

WHY THE FIELD SET IS CLOSED, AND WHY IT HAS EXACTLY ONE MEMBER. §9.1.1 step 2 has the KMS extract 'the claimed `policy_bundle_hash` and `bundle_epoch`' from every signing request. Both are already inside the bytes below, because both are receipt fields (§9.2). Carrying them AGAIN beside those bytes would give one value two spellings, and the two spellings are separately chosen by the party under verification. A compromised Policy Engine puts the current epoch and the current bundle hash in the request fields -- which is what the KMS retrieves, verifies and checks against its high-water mark (steps 3-5) -- and a superseded, genuinely signed, more permissive bundle's hash and epoch in the body it hands over. Every step of §9.1.1 passes, and the KMS then signs, under the one key the Executor trusts, a receipt naming a bundle it never verified. That is not a subtle failure of the protocol: it is RAD-4 violated in the exact words RAD-4 uses, reached without the KMS breaking any rule it was given, because the rule was given about a different field. Downstream it is T-15 bundle rollback, and §9.3 step 4 is the only thing left in its way -- a comparison against the Executor's last-seen epoch, which ZIFFER-SPEC-001 never makes durable or shared (ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 DP-40 supplies that obligation and records the gap as a live one). `additionalProperties: false` with one required member is what forbids the second spelling, and it is the reason this artifact needs a schema at all rather than being left to the transport.

WHAT THE KMS DOES WITH THIS, SO THE SCHEMA IS NOT MISREAD AS AUTHORITY. Every value reachable through this field is a CLAIM by the Policy Engine, and RAD-4 is explicit that the KMS MUST NOT accept bundle metadata, epochs or policy hashes from the Policy Engine runtime without cryptographic verification. The `policy_bundle_hash` in the body is a NAME for a bundle, never evidence of one: the KMS retrieves that bundle from the read-only repository the Policy Engine runtime cannot write to (§9.1.1 step 3, isolation stronger than filesystem permissions) and verifies its Ed25519 signature against its own copy of the `policy_signing_key` public key (step 4). On failure it rejects all signing requests until a valid bundle is presented (RAD-4). The `bundle_epoch` in the body is not authority either: RAD-3 compares it against the highest epoch the KMS has ever validated for that tenant in durable storage, rejects anything lower, and updates the mark (step 5). The mark is state at the KMS and appears in no message here. TR-10 states the general form -- a transmitted identifier is a name for a binding, not evidence of one.

WHAT IS NOT A FIELD, each absence with its reason. (a) No `policy_bundle_hash`, `bundle_epoch` or `tenant_id` beside the body: one value, one spelling, per the paragraph above; the tenant RAD-1, RAD-2 and RAD-3 are all scoped to is the body's `tenant_id` (§9.2). (b) No key identifier and no algorithm or suite selector: the Executor verifies under the `receipt_signing_key` the signed bundle registers (§9.3 step 1), so the key is settled by the bundle the KMS has just verified, not by the requester. Offering the party under verification a negotiable parameter is the downgrade shape AB-0 refuses one layer up, where accepting receipt versions 2 and 3 concurrently would let an attacker present the weaker one. (c) No canonical Proposal: §9.1.1 gives the KMS steps 2-5 and no policy evaluation. The KMS is independent about BUNDLE AUTHENTICITY, not about whether the Decision is correct, and §10's compromise table already grants that a compromised Policy Engine emits arbitrary Decision content, answering it with RAD-1/RAD-2 rate limits, the Executor's recomputation (TR-8) and audit replay. A Proposal on this leg would read as a second evaluation that no clause defines. (d) No attestation entries: under receipt version 3 they are excluded from the signed body by construction (AB-5), they reach the KMS from the approver devices on leg F4.4, and they travel beside the receipt on F3.3. (e) No `x-acp-absent` anywhere: no clause declares a fail-safe default for any part of this artifact, and inventing one would give an absent field a meaning the specification does not give it.

WHAT THIS SCHEMA DOES NOT CONSTRAIN, stated so the claim is not read wider than it is. It constrains SHAPE, and shape is not authority: under the §14 suite-12 classification every value reachable through this field is class T at the schema layer, and the receiving obligations are RAD-3 and RAD-4 exactly as the leg register cites them, not restated here (ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 DP-84). It says nothing about ORDER, and §9.1.1 is an ordered checklist: a KMS that signs first and verifies afterwards satisfies every line below. It says nothing about the durable high-water mark, which is per-tenant state and crosses no leg. It says nothing about freshness of the request itself -- no clause gives this leg an anti-replay value, and a replayed request re-signs the same body, whose duplicate is caught downstream only by CL-3's consumption of the receipt nonce. And it says nothing about the response: §9.1.1 step 7's `SIGNING_DENIED` is a normative reply with no schema here and no row in the leg register.

WHAT THE SPECIFICATION DOES NOT ANSWER. Recorded rather than filled in, because a schema that invents an answer publishes it as though the specification had one. (1) Who assembles `attestation_digests` (AB-1) is unstated, and the register gives the Policy Engine no leg on which attestation entries or their digests reach it -- F4.4 routes them to the KMS. If the KMS assembles them, this leg carries a PARTIAL body and this schema is wrong in shape rather than in detail. (2) §9.1.1 step 2 does not say whether the claimed values are separate request fields or are read out of the body; this schema takes the second reading and gives its reason above, but the text settles neither. (3) No clause names the party that canonicalizes the receipt body, nor forbids the KMS re-encoding a structure it decoded before signing; AT-8a states that rule for the Attestation Object only. (4) AB-6's 4,096-byte bound is written about the Executor, and no clause states it at this leg even though the bytes are the same bytes. (5) Nothing in this repository builds or consumes a signing request: `sim/receipts.py` plays the KMS and signs directly, there is no KMS-side epoch mark anywhere, and `tools/check-flow-legs.py` resolves this leg's RAD-3 citation against a raise site in the Executor and exempts RAD-4 outright. So the two obligations this leg cites have no executable consumer AT THIS BOUNDARY, which is the normative-text-with-no-executable-consumer shape ACP-50, ACP-56 and ACP-57 each landed a check for.

signed_body.description:
The bytes to be signed: the canonical CBOR encoding (RFC 8949 §4.2) of the receipt body WITHOUT the attestation entries (WE-1, WE-2, AB-5), carried as a WE-4 value.

THE NAME IS THE SPECIFICATION'S. AB-5, AB-6 and §9.3 step 7b all call these bytes 'the signed body', so calling them anything else here would be a second vocabulary for one object -- the defect ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 DP-16 forbids one layer down. At this leg the signature does not exist yet; the name is for the bytes the signature will cover, and no field here carries a signature.

THE KMS SIGNS THE BYTES IT RECEIVED. It parses them to extract the claimed `policy_bundle_hash` and `bundle_epoch` of §9.1.1 step 2, and signs the received encoding rather than a re-encoding of the structure it decoded. Two encoders on one signing path is the defect AT-8a names for the Attestation Object -- issuer and verifier disagree and one object acquires two identities -- and nothing about the receipt makes it immune, since the Executor recomputes nothing here and verifies the signature over the bytes it is handed (§9.3 step 1). WE-3 refuses JSON as receipt input for the same reason; it is written about a receipt consumer rather than about this leg, so it supports the rule here without stating it. Carrying bytes rather than a decoded object is also what makes 'the bytes signed are the bytes the Policy Engine composed' a checkable claim instead of an assumption.

THE LENGTH BOUND IS DERIVED, NOT CITED, AND IT IS NOT EXACT. AB-6 caps the signed body at 4,096 bytes and requires the check on MEASURED BYTES rather than on any proxy, having been written after a draft capped the digest count at 50 and measured 4,107 bytes at that cap. These are the bytes AB-6 bounds (AB-5), so a request over the cap asks for a receipt no conformant Executor may accept and no custody tier T2 key can produce -- the 4,096-byte limit is AWS KMS's `MessageType: RAW` cap, executed rather than read in `tools/kms-compat-2026-08-22.json` (5/5 PASS, 2026-08-22). `maxLength` here is on the base64 TEXT, and base64 quantizes at three bytes: 5,468 characters admits 4,098 bytes, two more than AB-6 allows. It is therefore a floor on refusal and never the check. An implementation MUST measure the decoded bytes, which is AB-6's own warning about proxies applied to AB-6's own transport encoding. No clause places the bound at this leg at all; that gap is recorded on the schema above rather than closed here.

EVERYTHING IN THESE BYTES IS A CLAIM. The KMS verifies the bundle they name (RAD-4) and the epoch they reference (RAD-3) against artifacts and state it holds itself; it does not verify the Decision they assert, and no clause asks it to.

b64_bytes.description:
A byte string carried as text under WE-4: the ASCII `"b64:"` followed by RFC 4648 §4 base64, WITH padding. The URL-safe alphabet (RFC 4648 §5) and unpadded encodings are different values and MUST be rejected rather than normalized.

The prefix is part of the value, not a label on it. §11.2 pins `sha256:` to the character and records why it had to -- an implementer who fed forward raw digest bytes built a different chain while following the text -- and WE-4 exists because the same hole was open on every `b64:` value through v1.3.17, where the string appeared only inside §9.2's diagnostic JSON and no clause said whether the prefix was part of what gets hashed and signed. Two spellings of one byte string are two values, and at a verifier the mismatch is indistinguishable from a forgery.

This type carries no length bound: WE-4 governs the encoding, and the size of any particular value is the business of the clause that defines it.
